paragraphs: We observe that for several centuries social conditions have been moving toward equality, and we find that over the same period the manners of society have grown milder. Are these two things merely simultaneous, or is there some hidden link between them, so that one cannot advance without driving the other forward? Several causes may combine to make a people’s manners less rough, but of all of them the most powerful seems to me to be equality of conditions. In my view, then, equality of conditions and increasing civility of manners are not only simultaneous but correlated facts. When fable writers want to interest us in the actions of animals, they give them human ideas and passions. The poets who sing of spirits and angels do the same. No misery is so deep, and no happiness so pure, that it can fill the human mind and touch the heart unless we ourselves are held up before our own eyes in some other form.

This applies exactly to the subject we are now considering. In an aristocratic community, all men are fixed irrevocably in their places by profession, property, and birth. The members of each class regard themselves as children of one family and feel a constant, lively sympathy for one another, which the citizens of a democracy can never feel to the same degree. But the several classes do not feel the same way toward one another. Among an aristocratic people, each caste has its own opinions, feelings, rights, manners, and ways of living. So the men of each caste do not resemble the mass of their fellow citizens. They do not think or feel in the same way, and they hardly believe that they belong to the same human race. They therefore cannot fully understand what others feel, or judge others by themselves. Yet they are sometimes eager to help one another, and this does not contradict my earlier remark. These aristocratic institutions made beings of one and the same race very different, but they nevertheless tied them to one another by close political bonds. The serf had no natural interest in the fate of nobles, yet he still thought himself obliged to devote his person to the service of whichever noble happened to be his lord. And although the noble considered himself of a different nature from his serfs, he nevertheless held that his duty and his honor required him to defend, at the risk of his own life, those who lived on his lands.

Clearly, these mutual obligations did not originate in the law of nature but in the law of society, and the claim of social duty was stronger than that of mere humanity. These services were not thought to be owed from one man to another, but to the vassal or to the lord. Feudal institutions awakened a lively sympathy for the sufferings of certain men, but none at all for the miseries of mankind. They gave the manners of the time generosity rather than gentleness. They prompted men to great acts of self-devotion, but they produced no real sympathies. For real sympathies can exist only between those who are alike, and in aristocratic ages men acknowledge no one but the members of their own caste to be like themselves.

When the chroniclers of the Middle Ages, all of whom belonged to the aristocracy by birth or education, tell of the tragic end of a noble, their grief flows freely. Yet they report in a single breath, and without flinching, the massacres and tortures inflicted on common people. It is not that these writers felt habitual hatred or systematic contempt for the people; war between the classes of the community had not yet been declared. Instinct drove them rather than passion. Since they had formed no clear idea of a poor man’s sufferings, they cared little about his fate. The same feelings moved the lower orders whenever the feudal tie was broken. The very ages that saw so many heroic acts of self-devotion by vassals for their lords were also stained by atrocious cruelties, committed from time to time by the lower classes against the higher. We must not suppose that this mutual insensibility arose solely from the lack of public order and education. Traces of it are found in later centuries, which became peaceful and enlightened while still remaining aristocratic. In 1675 the lower classes in Brittany rose in revolt against a new tax. The disturbances were put down with unparalleled atrocity. Observe the language in which Madame de Sevigne, a witness of these horrors, describes them to her daughter: —

“Mon Dieu, ma fille, que votre lettre d’Aix est plaisante! Au moins relisez vos lettres avant que de les envoyer; laissez-vous surpendre a leur agrement, et consolez-vous par ce plaisir de la peine que vous avez d’en tant ecrire. Vous avez donc baise toute la Provence? il n’y aurait pas satisfaction a baiser toute la Bretagne, a moins qu’on n’aimat a sentir le vin. . . . Voulez-vous savoir des nouvelles de Rennes? On a fait une taxe de cent mille ecus sur le bourgeois; et si on ne trouve point cette somme dans vingt-quatre heures, elle sera doublee et exigible par les soldats. On a chasse et banni toute une grand rue, et defendu de les recueillir sous peine de la vie; de sorte qu’on voyait tous ces miserables, veillards, femmes accouchees, enfans, errer en pleurs au sortir de cette ville sans savoir ou aller. On roua avant-hier un violon, qui avait commence la danse et la pillerie du papier timbre; il a ete ecartele apres sa mort, et ses quatre quartiers exposes aux quatre coins de la ville. On a pris soixante bourgeois, et on commence demain les punitions. Cette province est un bel exemple pour les autres, et surtout de respecter les gouverneurs et les gouvernantes, et de ne point jeter de pierres dans leur jardin.” *a

[Footnote a: To see the point of this joke, the reader should remember that Madame de Grignan was Gouvernante de Provence.] “Madame de Tarente etait hier dans ces bois par un temps enchante: il n’est question ni de chambre ni de collation; elle entre par la barriere et s’en retourne de meme. . . .”

“Vous me parlez bien plaisamment de nos miseres; nous ne sommes plus si roues; un en huit jours, pour entretenir la justice. Il est vrai que la penderie me parait maintenant un refraichissement. J’ai une tout autre idee de la justice, depuis que je suis en ce pays. Vos galeriens me paraissent une societe d’honnetes gens qui se sont retires du monde pour mener une vie douce.”

Do not conclude that Madame de Sevigne, the author of these lines, was a selfish or cruel woman. She adored her children and was quick to share her friends’ sorrows. Her letters even show that she was kind and indulgent toward her vassals and servants. Yet she had no clear idea that anyone could suffer who was not a person of quality.

In our time, even the harshest man, writing to the most unfeeling person he knows, would not dare to indulge so wantonly in the cruel joking I have quoted. And even if his own manners permitted it, the manners of society at large would forbid it. Where does this come from? Are we more sensitive than our forefathers? I do not know that we are, but I am sure that our insensibility extends to a far greater range of objects. When all the ranks of a community are nearly equal, all men think and feel in nearly the same way, and each of them can judge in a moment the sensations of all the others. He glances quickly at himself, and that is enough. There is no wretchedness he cannot readily enter into, and a secret instinct tells him how great it is. It does not matter whether the sufferers are strangers or enemies; imagination puts him in their place. Something like a personal feeling mingles with his pity and makes him suffer while his fellow creature’s body is being tortured. In democratic ages men rarely sacrifice themselves for one another, but they show a general compassion for all members of the human race. They inflict no needless harm, and they are glad to relieve the griefs of others when they can do so without hurting themselves much. They are not disinterested, but they are humane.

Although the Americans have in a manner reduced egotism to a social and philosophical theory, they are nonetheless very open to compassion. In no country is criminal justice administered more mildly than in the United States. While the English seem intent on carefully preserving the bloody traces of the dark ages in their penal laws, the Americans have almost erased capital punishment from their codes. North America is, I think, the only country on earth where no citizen’s life has been taken for a political offense in the last fifty years. What conclusively shows that this unusual mildness of the Americans arises chiefly from their social condition is the way they treat their slaves. Perhaps there is not, on the whole, a single European colony in the New World where the physical condition of Black people is less harsh than in the United States. Yet the slaves there still endure horrible sufferings and are constantly exposed to barbarous punishments. It is easy to see that the lot of these unfortunate beings inspires little compassion in their masters, who regard slavery not only as an institution that profits them but as an evil that does not touch them. Thus the same man who is full of humanity toward his fellow creatures when they are also his equals becomes insensible to their afflictions as soon as that equality ends. His mildness should therefore be attributed to equality of conditions rather than to civilization and education.

What I have observed here of individuals applies, to a certain extent, to nations. When each nation has its own distinct opinions, beliefs, laws, and customs, it regards itself as the whole of mankind and is moved by no sorrows but its own. If war breaks out between two nations with this feeling, it is sure to be waged with great cruelty. At the height of their culture, the Romans slaughtered their enemies’ generals after dragging them in triumph behind a chariot, and they threw their prisoners to the beasts of the Circus to amuse the people. Cicero, who spoke so vehemently against the idea of crucifying a Roman citizen, had not a word to say against these horrible abuses of victory. Clearly, in his eyes a barbarian did not belong to the same human race as a Roman. On the contrary, as nations become more like one another, they grow more compassionate toward each other, and the law of nations is softened.
